title: What Your Black Friday Change Freeze Says About Your Databases
summary: Your Black Friday change freeze list is the most honest database infrastructure audit you'll write all year. Here's what to record across the Cyber 5.
body_markdown:
### Summary


Your Black Friday change freeze can reveal more than operational caution. It can expose infrastructure limitations affecting database performance, availability, and recovery. Recording what happens across the Cyber 5, from the first Thanksgiving spike to the 3 a.m. page, turns that list into next year’s roadmap.


Database teams running a change freeze this week are working from a list of what it won’t touch until after Cyber Monday: the firmware update, the capacity expansion, the array migration that has already slipped twice.


In many organizations, that list gets filed away in January without anyone asking why each item landed on it, which can waste the most accurate assessment of database infrastructure the team will produce all year. Capacity plans and architecture reviews describe what a team expects its infrastructure to handle. The freeze list, meanwhile, can reveal where storage upgrades, capacity expansion, or other routine infrastructure changes still introduce unacceptable operational risk.The weekend that follows is the one production-scale load test nobody has to schedule.


The question isn’t whether organizations should freeze risky changes during Black Friday. It’s whether routine storage operations should create additional risk for the databases keeping the business running.


That test gets harder every year. Between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. on Black Friday 2025, U.S. shoppers spent an average of $12.5 million online every minute,[according to Adobe](https://www.digitalcommerce360.com/article/black-friday-ecommerce-sales/) , and a single global commerce platform ran 14.8 trillion database queries between Black Friday and Cyber Monday. This year[Adobe expects Black Friday to grow faster](https://news.adobe.com/news/2026/09/adobe-us-holiday-shopping-season-to-hit-record) than Cyber Monday and reach $12.9 billion in U.S. online sales, with Cyber Monday forecast to become the first U.S. online shopping day above $15 billion.


By this point in November, nothing on the list is going to change before the traffic arrives. What a team can still do is watch the weekend closely and write down what it sees, so that by January the freeze list comes with evidence attached.


## **Six weeks out, the freeze list shows where the team stopped trusting its storage**


A multi-national commerce company, which has more peak-day practice than most, states the principle plainly: “We don’t use BFCM as a release deadline.” Its engineering team starts preparing in March, runs fire drills at 150% of the previous year’s peak load and holds game days that inject database latency on purpose, so very little is left to freeze by November. Most enterprise estates reach the freeze with a longer list, and its items are frozen for different reasons. Some items carry change risk, meaning the change itself is dangerous during peak traffic, such as new application code or a schema change on the orders table. Others expose infrastructure-related risk: a storage controller upgrade requiring downtime, a capacity expansion involving data migration, or a storage refresh that triggers extensive database revalidation. These are operational constraints that a modern data storage platform should help minimize.


Platform risk is expensive in ways that rarely show up on a budget line. In the Everpure™[State of Database Infrastructure 2026](https://www.everpuredata.com/resources/type-a/state-of-database-infrastructure.html) research report with Vanson Bourne, database teams reported spending 19% of their time revalidating systems after upgrades and migrations, and 70% of organizations said downtime is no longer acceptable even when it’s planned. Before the weekend starts, go down the freeze list and tag each item as change risk or platform risk. The notes worth taking over the rest of the weekend get the same tags.


## **Thanksgiving night, record tail latency, because the average will look fine**


Peak traffic no longer waits for Friday morning. Adobe’s 2026 forecast names Thanksgiving as the strongest mobile shopping day of the season, with 63% of Cyber Week spending expected to come from mobile devices.


Averages hide what happens during these steps. Storage can report excellent average latency while individual requests stall as queues deepen, and a shopper whose cart read hangs for two seconds experiences only that one request. Capture storage latency, including p99 latency where available, alongside IOPS, throughput, and queue depth during peak transaction periods. Correlate these measurements with database and application response times to determine whether storage is contributing to performance degradation. If it took a month of query retuning, or capacity bought for four days a year, that cost belongs on the list next to the latency figure.


## **Black Friday at noon, note every workload someone had to pause by hand**


The busiest hour of the year is rarely spent on checkout alone. Backups run longer because there is more data to protect, merchandising teams refresh their dashboards constantly, and fraud scoring, inventory sync and replication all run alongside the transactions that bring in revenue.


On shared storage any of them can push latency up for the others, and the usual fix of running full backups in a quiet window fails when the weekend has no quiet window. Teams end up managing contention by hand, pausing a report here and pushing a backup there, and those calls almost never get written down. Record each intervention, including which workload was paused, for how long, and why. If teams repeatedly throttle reporting, analytics, or backup workloads to protect checkout performance, investigate whether storage contention is contributing to the problem and whether workload-level quality-of-service controls could reduce the need for manual intervention.


## **Saturday at 3 a.m., time every recovery, including the small ones**


Something will break over the weekend, usually at the least convenient hour and in front of an on-call engineer who has been watching dashboards since Thursday.


The cost is high even on an ordinary day: in[Uptime Institute’s 2025 survey](https://intelligence.uptimeinstitute.com/resource/annual-outage-analysis-2026) , 57% of respondents said their most recent major outage cost more than $100,000, and one in five put the figure above $1 million. Most teams know their recovery time objectives from a planning document, and far fewer know how long recovery took the last time it happened under real load. Whether recovering from an array failure, restoring data from a storage snapshot, or bringing a database back online, record the actual recovery time against the established recovery time objective (RTO). Also capture any data loss against the recovery point objective (RPO). When budget conversations start in January, a gap between those two numbers carries more weight than anything else on the list.


## **In December, sort the list and plan from the platform-risk items**


When the freeze lifts, the deferred work comes due, and that is the time to read the list again with the weekend’s notes added. A typical one might look like this:


**On the freeze list** **Why** **Tag**


Release the new checkout recommendations service New application code during peak traffic Change risk


Controller upgrade on the orders array Needs a maintenance window and a week of revalidation Platform risk


Capacity expansion for the reporting array Means migrating data first Platform risk


Thanksgiving, 9:40 p.m.: p99 latency on the checkout array tripled for 20 minutes Contained only by capacity bought for the weekend Platform risk


Black Friday, 12:20 p.m.: paused finance reports for 90 minutes Reporting queries were slowing checkout Platform risk


Saturday, 3:10 a.m.: restored a corrupted volume Took 2 hours against a 30-minute objective Platform risk


The one change-risk item stays on next year’s freeze, because no infrastructure removes the risk of shipping new code in the middle of Cyber Monday. The remaining items point to infrastructure limitations worth investigating, from disruptive storage maintenance to workload contention and recovery delays. Addressing these constraints can reduce the number of routine infrastructure changes that must be deferred during next year’s peak season.. Next November’s goal is a freeze that only has to cover the change-risk items.


Sorting the platform-risk items by cost gives the roadmap its order. Recoveries that ran past their objectives go first, because they are the most expensive gaps if they repeat on a bigger day. Manual throttles come next, since they will recur at every peak until the storage can enforce limits on its own. Maintenance-window items go last: they are painful but predictable, and they stop needing a freeze once the storage can be upgraded and expanded without downtime.


Many of these infrastructure risks can be reduced through a modern storage and data management platform. Everpure FlashArray™, built on Evergreen® architecture, enables non-disruptive storage upgrades and capacity expansion, helping organizations modernize their database infrastructure without introducing planned storage downtime or recurring disruptive refresh cycles. Storage-level quality-of-service controls help limit contention between competing workloads, while space-efficient snapshots and cloning enable rapid creation of database copies for backup, testing, and reporting workflows when integrated with database-aware processes.Synchronous replication through ActiveCluster™ keeps a database running through the loss of an array, and when a restore from backup can’t be avoided, restore speed is what closes the distance between the recovery plan and the recovery itself. In Everpure testing, Oracle RMAN restores to a two-node RAC cluster from Everpure FlashBlade ran at more than 60TB an hour, enough to[bring a 10TB database back in about 10 minutes](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/recovery-speed-database-scale/) .


## **This week, four notes turn the freeze into next year’s plan**


Most teams reading this are already inside their freeze, which makes this the right week to start. Four notes cover the weekend:


- The reason behind every frozen change, tagged change risk or platform risk
- p99 latency on the arrays carrying checkout at the busiest points of the weekend
- Every workload someone paused or throttled by hand, with how long and who decided
- The real elapsed time of every recovery, set against its objective


Once the list is sorted, compare its platform-risk items with the[State of Database Infrastructure 2026 findings](https://www.everpuredata.com/resources/type-a/state-of-database-infrastructure.html) from 500 infrastructure leaders across six countries. If the platform-risk list turns out to be long, bring it to your Everpure team, who can walk through it item by item and show which entries a storage platform built for non-disruptive change would take off next year’s list.
